A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same General Policy Composition (GPC) study. Their main text, equations, proofs, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Robomimic, PushT, RoboTwin, and four real-world tasks, including detailed appendix weight sweeps.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds inference-latency measurements, heterogeneous-chunk results, and three-policy composition results in Tables 7–9.

M1.justification: The core convex score-composition method remains unchanged. v2 introduces an optional restricted weight search favoring the stronger policy and an unequal-chunk adaptation that combines overlapping scores while retaining the longer policy's tail. Three-policy composition uses the existing general formula.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Robomimic tasks, PushT, RoboTwin task subsets, and four real-world tasks. The added experiments vary policy configurations within this coverage. New prompt examples document the existing RoboTwin VLA setup.

E2.justification: Table 9 introduces best two-policy GPC as an explicit comparator for three-policy composition. The baseline membership in the original benchmark comparisons and corresponding appendix tables remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluations include DP with DDPM, chunk length 8, and 5 inference steps versus Florence-Policy-D with DDIM, chunk length 16, and 10 steps; composition uses the latter configuration (Table 8). v2 also adds three-policy evaluation and per-chunk latency measurement. Existing benchmark training and rollout protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 6.4–6.5 substantially broaden the supplementary analysis to address search and inference costs, compatibility with heterogeneous chunk lengths and sampling configurations, and scaling beyond pairwise composition (Tables 6–9). Existing weight sweeps, operator comparisons, and visualization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The existing RoboTwin 1.0 seed-0 disclosure remains unchanged. Neither version provides confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-seed summaries; the new results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and appendix result values are unchanged. New Tables 6–9 report estimated search costs of approximately 2.5 versus 1 hour, GPC latency of 0.13 seconds per chunk, heterogeneous-configuration success rates of 0.66 versus 0.50/0.53, and three-policy results of 1.00/1.00/0.94. These are additional results, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under matched settings.

T1.justification: Corollary 4.1 and Appendix D replace v1's claim of strictly smaller actual expected terminal trajectory error with a claim of a strictly smaller theoretical error bound, rewriting the proof accordingly. Proposition 4.1 also softens its strict-improvement statement, and Appendix B adds an interior-optimum qualification. This materially narrows the central theoretical guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: training-free heterogeneous policy composition, theoretical motivation, and broad empirical improvements. Despite the narrowed corollary, these passages still describe propagation of single-step advantages into trajectory or system-level gains.

C2.justification: New Appendix H elaborates mechanisms involving RGB versus geometric information, architectural inductive biases, and task-dependent policy strengths. Section 6.4 interprets computational costs, while the limitations now acknowledge dual/triple-policy experiments. These extend the existing interpretation without replacing it.

D1.justification: Appendix I.3 newly documents RoboTwin task schemas and training/test prompt paraphrases. v2 also supplies rollout-duration and search-cost assumptions, sampler/chunk alignment instructions, and per-action noise-initialization clarification in Algorithm 1. Existing training hyperparameters, robot hardware descriptions, and access links are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Snell et al. (2024) on test-time computation and Liu et al. (2026), RDT2, in the efficiency discussion and references. The main related-work positioning, including the comparison with PoCo, and the extensive literature-review appendix remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 adds an efficiency subsection and explanatory Appendix H, revises selected theoretical and experimental passages, and updates the publication header and author footnotes. Subsequent appendices are relabeled, but the overall narrative and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Four new tables are inserted as Tables 6–9, and Figure 2 moves from page 4 to page 3. Other floats and surrounding text reflow. All original figures and tables are retained; appendix Tables 6–20 become Tables 10–24 without substantive display changes.

improvement.justification: Narrowing Corollary 4.1 partially repairs an important theoretical overclaim, while the new timing, compatibility, and three-policy results improve assessment of practical applicability. The gain is limited: the abstract, conclusion, and new Appendix H still imply stronger trajectory guarantees, and Table 9's π0 Can result of 0.61 is not reconciled with the retained Table 1 value of 96.50%. Overall, the additions provide useful but qualified improvements in rigor and evidence.
